title: Nursing IQ
disclaimer: Six-question prototype content for Nursing IQ. This prototype evaluates clinical judgment patterns in addition to answer correctness.

instructions.title: Student Instructions
body: Nursing IQ evaluates more than whether you select the correct answer. The assessment examines how you recognize clinical information, interpret findings, establish priorities, identify solutions, select nursing actions, and evaluate outcomes.

For each question, select the best answer or answers. Some questions require more than one response. Rate your confidence before submitting. On selected questions, you will also be asked what influenced your decision. Your response time will be recorded automatically. There is no individual question time limit. Please do not use outside resources.
There is no penalty for uncertainty. Answer honestly.

questions.prompt: A 67-year-old patient is 6 hours postoperative following total hip arthroplasty. Temperature 37.4 C (99.3 F), HR 112/min, RR 26/min, BP 108/68 mmHg, SpO2 89% on room air, new restlessness, sudden shortness of breath, and incisional pain 5/10. Which findings require immediate follow-up? Select all that apply.

correct.heading: Correct.
body: You recognized the priority clinical cues.
Sudden dyspnea, hypoxemia, tachypnea, tachycardia, and new restlessness together indicate acute respiratory deterioration requiring prompt evaluation.

sections.title: Nursing IQ Teaching Point
sections.body: Abnormal does not always mean immediate priority. Look for findings that are new, unexpected, changing, and potentially unstable. Ask: Which findings suggest that the patient's condition could deteriorate if care is delayed?

sections.title: Replace the Rule
sections.body: Instead of: Abnormal equals urgent. Think: Identify abnormality, determine clinical significance, then compare urgency.

sections.title: Clinical Judgment Analysis
sections.body: Domain: Recognize Cues. This response provides preliminary information about your ability to distinguish immediately relevant clinical information from other patient findings.

partial.heading: Partially correct.
body: You're on the right track, but let's look more closely.
You identified some of the concerning findings but either missed an important cue or selected a finding that does not have the same immediate priority.

sections.title: Why Not F?
sections.body: Incisional pain requires assessment and management, but moderate postoperative pain does not represent the same immediate physiologic threat as new respiratory compromise.

sections.title: Nursing IQ Teaching Point
sections.body: Abnormal does not always mean immediate priority. Look for findings that are new, unexpected, changing, and potentially unstable.

sections.title: Clinical Judgment Analysis
sections.body: Domain: Recognize Cues. Nursing IQ will look for this pattern across additional questions before identifying a consistent strength or area for development.

incorrect.heading: Not quite.
body: Let's examine the clinical picture.
The priority findings are A, B, C, D, and E. Taken together, these findings indicate acute respiratory deterioration.

sections.title: Why Not F?
sections.body: Incisional pain requires assessment and management, but moderate postoperative pain does not represent the same immediate physiologic threat as new respiratory compromise.

sections.title: Nursing IQ Teaching Point
sections.body: Abnormal does not always mean immediate priority. Look for findings that are new, unexpected, changing, and potentially unstable.

sections.title: Clinical Judgment Analysis
sections.body: Domain: Recognize Cues. One incorrect response alone does not establish a consistent cue-recognition deficit.

questions.prompt: A patient with type 1 diabetes receives rapid-acting insulin before breakfast but eats only a few bites. Thirty minutes later the patient is diaphoretic, trembling, dizzy, HR 110/min, and blood glucose 52 mg/dL. Which interpretation best explains these findings?
options: Hypoglycemia associated with insulin administration and inadequate carbohydrate intake
Expected medication effects requiring no intervention
thinkingOptions: The relationship between insulin and food intake
I wasn't sure how the findings fit together

correct.heading: Correct.
body: You successfully connected the clinical cues.
Rapid-acting insulin, inadequate carbohydrate intake, autonomic symptoms, and a blood glucose of 52 mg/dL form a consistent pattern of hypoglycemia.

sections.title: Nursing IQ Teaching Point
sections.body: Cluster your cues. Ask: What explanation accounts for the greatest number of findings?

sections.title: Replace the Rule
sections.body: Instead of: Interpret each finding separately. Think: Combine related findings to identify the clinical pattern.

sections.title: Clinical Judgment Analysis
sections.body: Domain: Analyze Cues. Nursing IQ distinguishes content knowledge gaps from cue-analysis reasoning patterns because they require different remediation.

incorrect.heading: Not quite.
body: The best answer is B.
Rather than considering each finding separately, examine how the medication, food intake, symptoms, and objective glucose measurement relate to one another.

sections.title: Why Not?
sections.body: A: The measured glucose is low, not elevated. C: Anxiety could cause some similar symptoms but does not adequately explain documented hypoglycemia in this context. D: Symptomatic hypoglycemia requires intervention.

sections.title: Nursing IQ Teaching Point
sections.body: Cluster your cues. Ask: What explanation accounts for the greatest number of findings?

sections.title: Clinical Judgment Analysis
sections.body: Domain: Analyze Cues. If you understood insulin but did not connect the medication, food intake, symptoms, and glucose level, this may indicate a cue-analysis reasoning pattern.

questions.prompt: The nurse receives report on four patients. Which patient should the nurse assess first?
options: Heart failure patient with 2-lb overnight weight gain and ankle edema
Postoperative patient following IV opioid administration with RR 8/min, SpO2 87%, and increasing somnolence
Patient awaiting discharge with medication questions

correct.heading: Correct.
body: You identified the patient with the greatest immediate threat.
Respiratory depression, hypoxemia, and increasing somnolence following opioid administration require immediate attention.

sections.title: Nursing IQ Teaching Point
sections.body: Do not ask only: Who has a problem? Ask: Who could experience the greatest harm if I delay?

sections.title: Replace the Rule
sections.body: Instead of: Serious diagnosis equals priority. Think: Current physiologic instability helps determine priority.

sections.title: Clinical Judgment Analysis
sections.body: Domain: Prioritize Hypotheses. One response alone does not establish a prioritization pattern, but repeated responses can reveal whether urgent instability is being recognized.

incorrect.heading: Not quite.
body: You identified a patient who needs care, but not the patient who needs care first.
Patient C has evidence of an immediate ventilation and oxygenation problem that could rapidly progress if intervention is delayed.

sections.title: Why Not?
sections.body: A: Fluid retention requires assessment but does not indicate the same immediate instability. B: Pain requires treatment but is not the greatest immediate threat presented. D: Education can safely be delayed.

sections.title: Nursing IQ Teaching Point
sections.body: Compare immediate threat versus potential threat, acute deterioration versus chronic or expected findings, and unstable versus currently stable.

sections.title: Clinical Judgment Analysis
sections.body: Domain: Prioritize Hypotheses. If this pattern recurs, Nursing IQ may identify difficulty distinguishing an important problem from the most urgent problem.

questions.prompt: A 74-year-old patient with acute heart failure has increasing dyspnea, RR 28/min, SpO2 88%, bilateral crackles, 2+ lower-extremity edema, and increased work of breathing. Which interventions are appropriate components of the immediate plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: Closely monitor respiratory status and oxygen saturation
thinkingOptions: Whether the interventions directly address the current problems
Interventions commonly associated with heart failure

correct.heading: Correct.
body: You selected interventions addressing the patient's respiratory compromise and fluid congestion.

sections.title: Nursing IQ Teaching Point
sections.body: Use: problem, desired outcome, intervention. Ask: Does this intervention directly address the problem I identified?

sections.title: Replace the Rule
sections.body: Instead of: This sounds like good nursing care. Think: Does this intervention address this patient's specific problem?

sections.title: Clinical Judgment Analysis
sections.body: Domain: Generate Solutions. Nursing IQ examines whether you can move from understanding the clinical problem to identifying appropriate solutions.

partial.heading: Partially correct.
body: You're on the right track.
You identified some appropriate interventions but either missed an intervention addressing the current problem or selected an intervention that could worsen it.

sections.title: Why Not?
sections.body: C: Additional fluid intake is inconsistent with acute fluid overload. F: Flat positioning may worsen respiratory distress.

sections.title: Nursing IQ Teaching Point
sections.body: Use: problem, desired outcome, intervention. Ask whether each intervention directly addresses the current problem.

sections.title: Clinical Judgment Analysis
sections.body: Domain: Generate Solutions. This response helps identify whether the gap is problem recognition, solution generation, or selecting generally helpful actions that do not match this situation.

incorrect.heading: Not quite.
body: The immediate plan should address respiratory compromise and fluid congestion.

The appropriate components are A, B, D, and E: position upright, provide supplemental oxygen as indicated or prescribed, administer prescribed diuretic therapy, and closely monitor respiratory status and oxygen saturation.

sections.title: Why Not?
sections.body: Additional oral fluids can worsen acute fluid overload, and flat positioning may worsen respiratory distress.

sections.title: Nursing IQ Teaching Point
sections.body: Use: problem, desired outcome, intervention. Choose interventions that directly address this patient's specific problem.

sections.title: Clinical Judgment Analysis
sections.body: Domain: Generate Solutions. Nursing IQ examines whether you can move from understanding the clinical problem to identifying appropriate solutions.

questions.prompt: A patient with type 1 diabetes becomes shaky, diaphoretic, and weak. The patient is awake and able to swallow, HR 108/min, BP 126/74 mmHg, and blood glucose 48 mg/dL. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Give 15 g of rapid-acting carbohydrate according to the hypoglycemia protocol
thinkingOptions: What the nurse can appropriately do immediately
I'm not sure how hypoglycemia is treated

correct.heading: Correct.
body: You correctly selected the immediate intervention for a conscious patient who can swallow and has symptomatic hypoglycemia.

sections.title: Nursing IQ Teaching Point
sections.body: Before choosing notify the provider, ask: Is there an appropriate nursing intervention I should initiate now?

sections.title: Replace the Rule
sections.body: Instead of: Serious problem means notify. Use: recognize problem, immediate appropriate nursing action, reassess, escalate as indicated.

sections.title: Clinical Judgment Analysis
sections.body: Domain: Take Action. Nursing IQ distinguishes knowledge gaps from action-selection reasoning patterns because they should not receive identical remediation.

incorrect.heading: Not quite.
body: The patient needs treatment now. The best response is B.
Give 15 g of rapid-acting carbohydrate according to the hypoglycemia protocol.

sections.title: Why Not?
sections.body: A: Notification should not unnecessarily delay indicated treatment. C: Insulin could worsen hypoglycemia. D: Waiting without treatment risks further deterioration.

sections.title: Nursing IQ Teaching Point
sections.body: Before choosing notify the provider, ask whether there is an appropriate nursing intervention you should initiate now.

sections.title: Clinical Judgment Analysis
sections.body: Domain: Take Action. This question can distinguish between not knowing the treatment and thinking the provider should be notified before immediate nursing action.

questions.prompt: A patient experiencing an acute asthma exacerbation receives prescribed bronchodilator therapy. Before treatment: RR 30/min, SpO2 89%, increased work of breathing, and difficulty speaking in complete sentences. Which finding provides the strongest evidence that treatment was effective?
options: RR decreases to 18/min, SpO2 increases to 96%, work of breathing improves, and patient speaks comfortably in complete sentences
thinkingOptions: Improvement in how the patient feels

correct.heading: Correct.
body: You correctly connected the intervention with measurable improvement in the problem being treated.
The patient's respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, work of breathing, and ability to speak all demonstrate improvement in respiratory function.

sections.title: Nursing IQ Teaching Point
sections.body: Ask: What was the intervention intended to improve? Then identify the finding that most directly demonstrates improvement in that problem.

sections.title: Replace the Rule
sections.body: Instead of: Positive change equals effective treatment. Think: Improvement in the targeted problem equals stronger evidence of effectiveness.

sections.title: Clinical Judgment Analysis
sections.body: Domain: Evaluate Outcomes. Nursing IQ examines whether you can connect an intervention to the specific outcome it was intended to produce.

incorrect.heading: Not quite.
body: A finding can be positive without being the best evidence that treatment worked.
The best answer is C. Respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, work of breathing, and ability to speak all demonstrate improvement in respiratory function.

sections.title: Why Not?
sections.body: A: Reduced anxiety is encouraging but less direct evidence. B: Heart rate alone is insufficient. D: Requesting water does not directly measure treatment effectiveness.

sections.title: Nursing IQ Teaching Point
sections.body: Ask what the intervention was intended to improve, then choose the finding that most directly demonstrates improvement in that problem.

sections.title: Clinical Judgment Analysis
sections.body: Domain: Evaluate Outcomes. Nursing IQ examines whether you can connect an intervention to the specific outcome it was intended to produce.
